extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of philosophy of science, mathematics, and epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the certainty of mathematical and scientific propositions, the status of deduction and induction, and the reliability of tests like inconceivability or uniformity of experience. Focuses on when deductions are hypothetical, what warrants belief, and how to test assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty limited to pure Number
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly called mathematical certainty — unconditional truth and perfect accuracy — is not an attribute of all mathematical truths, but of those only which relate to pure Number, as distinguished from Quantity in the more enlarged sense; and only so long as we abstain from supposing that the numbers are a precise index to actual quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If arithmetic is used only to count objects (number as an abstract index), conclusions can be treated as exactly true. When arithmetic is used to infer equality/inequality in other respects (e.g., weight, length), additional hypothetical assumptions (e.g., that units are equivalent) are required and exact certainty is lost. Examples: differing pound standards, horse strength, measured miles; statistics where only numbering matters remain exact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive sciences are fundamentally hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of all Deductive Sciences is hypothetical: they proceed by tracing the consequences of certain assumptions, leaving for separate consideration whether the assumptions are true or not, and if not exactly true, whether they are a sufficiently near approximation to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation must separate (a) the derivation of consequences from assumptions (which can be carried out once and catalogued) and (b) the empirical or argumentative task of testing the truth/adequacy of those assumptions in each application. Demonstrative science consists in working out implications of assumptions so they are ready to use when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions must be tested for degree of truth in each case
rubrics_metrics.description: Since in most deductive investigations assumptions are not exactly true (except in pure number cases), it must form part of the inquiry to determine how much the assumptions want of being exactly true in the case in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test is generally empirical (observation repeated for each new case) or, if by argument, will require case-specific evidence. The degree of approximation acceptable must be assessed per application; different cases may demand different evidence and present varying difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction can validly proceed from fictitious premises to yield consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is practicable to arrive at new conclusions from facts assumed, as from facts observed; from fictitious, as from real, inductions. Deduction consists of tracing consequences of suppositions, which may themselves be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deductions from false assumptions can still be useful (e.g., Ptolemaic, Cartesian models) either as explanatory devices or to expose assumption falsity via reductio ad absurdum. Recognize when a system is being explored hypothetically rather than asserted as true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reductio ad absurdum to test assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: One may assume premises to deduce consequences so as to show the falsity of an assumption by deriving contradiction (reductio ad absurdum): assume A→B→C, suppose C→D, but D contradicts A, therefore C is not a mark of D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reductio is a legitimate method to refute premises by exposing contradictions; it can be used knowingly to demonstrate the falsity of the starting assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination is not ultimately grounded in reductio alone
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been held that all ratiocination rests on reductio ad absurdum, but this is inadmissible: if someone denies the validity of a reasoning process, a reductio forces through another ratiocination, and so on; ultimately the foundation is the maxim that whatever has a mark, has what it is a mark of (or in universal form, transitivity of marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat reductio as the final ground for reasoning. Evaluation of arguments should acknowledge the foundational axioms or maxims (e.g., the mark axiom) that ratiocination presumes; disagreements about the reasoning process itself cannot be settled by chaining reductios without appealing to such axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conception/inconceivability from belief/unbelievability
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconceivable has a double meaning: (a) inability to form or bring together an idea (unimaginable), and (b) inability to form or sustain a belief (unbelievable). These two must be kept distinct when using inconceivability as a test of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antipodes were imaginable (one can picture people on the opposite side of the earth) but unbelievable given certain preconceptions; attempting to conceive an end to extension is literally unimaginable. Clarity about which sense is intended is essential in arguments relying on 'inconceivability'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability of a proposition's negation is not a reliable test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The inconceivableness of the negation of a proposition is not, by itself, proof of the proposition's truth; inconceivableness may arise from causes other than uniform past experience (e.g., tradition, strong associative connections, limited modes of representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat inability to imagine or believe the contrary as conclusive evidence. The cause of inconceivability must be investigated: it may reflect a superficial habit of thought or associative conditioning rather than genuine universal experience. Use counterexamples such as historical shifts (e.g., geocentric intuitions) as cautionary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of past experience is the proper substantive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a belief corresponds to the aggregate of all past experience (uniformity of experience), that uniformity is the substantive proof; inconceivability, at best, is only an incidental symptom of such uniformity, not its substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, state and rest beliefs on the uniformity of observed experience directly, and then evaluate how strong that evidence is in the particular case. Uniform experience varies in strength as evidence (from very strong to negligible); historical counterexamples (metals sinking until potassium discovered; all swans white until Australia) show its fallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer evidential force from inconceivability when direct evidence is available
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inconceivableness of a proposition is thought to represent agreement of pre-existing experience, the real evidence is that uniformity of experience itself, which is directly accessible and should be used rather than the incidental test of inconceivability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the uniformity of experience and weigh its probative value case-by-case instead of relying on the psychological inability to conceive alternatives. This clarifies what the evidence is and allows proper assessment of its strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of the same axiom in many inference steps does not multiply chance of error
rubrics_metrics.description: If successive steps of an argument all rely on the very same axiom, then repeating that same assumption many times does not create multiple independent chances of error; it is one chance of error, not many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rebuts the claim that long deductive chains are intrinsically less reliable simply because they 're-invoke' the universal postulate at each step. New and distinct premises introduced mid-argument are what increase susceptibility to error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate momentary conception from settled belief when assessing invariability
rubrics_metrics.description: Momentary inability to 'get rid of an idea' (e.g., vivid imagining provoked by circumstances) does not imply an invariable or settled belief; evaluation of whether a belief 'invariably exists' in a person or community must consider overall disposition, not transient imaginative states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a person frightened as an infant may have recurring imaginative reactions (ghosts) yet, on balance, disbelieve ghosts; skeptics of the external world may have momentary involuntary perceptions suggesting externality but still be disbelievers. Do not conflate temporary psychologic impulses with epistemic commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of conclusions depends both on truth of suppositions and completeness of data
rubrics_metrics.description: The certainty usually ascribed to geometry or mechanics is only 'certainty of inference': we can have full assurance of particular results under particular suppositions, but not the same assurance that these suppositions are accurately true, nor that they include all data that may influence the result in any given instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating theories or models, explicitly assess (a) how warranted the initial suppositions are, and (b) whether all relevant data have been included. High logical certainty of deduction does not guarantee real-world truth unless the premises and data adequacy are separately verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic conclusions require assumption that units are equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: In all propositions concerning numbers, a condition is implied — that all numbers are numbers of the same or of equal units (e.g., that '1=1' in the relevant unit sense); without this assumption, arithmetic propositions concerning quantities may be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying arithmetic to physical quantities or heterogeneous units, make explicit the assumption of unit-equivalence. Examples: adding a troy pound to an avoirdupois pound may not produce 'two pounds' in a coherent unit sense; comparing 'forty-horse power' presumes horses of equal strength. For statistical counts where only number matters (population), this assumption is unnecessary.
